sources.title: MySQL 8.4 InnoDB Clustered and Secondary Indexes

claims.text: MySQL 8.4 CREATE TABLE syntax supports INDEX/KEY, PRIMARY KEY, UNIQUE, FULLTEXT and SPATIAL definitions; KEY is normally synonymous with INDEX, an index may contain multiple key parts, and the index_type grammar exposes USING BTREE or HASH.

MySQL 8.4 states that only some storage engines permit an index type to be specified, so USING BTREE/HASH syntax must not be generalized into a claim that every storage engine supports both access methods.

MySQL 8.4 documents that index entries help locate rows matching WHERE conditions, while unnecessary indexes waste space and every index adds insert, update and delete maintenance cost; the optimizer decides whether a concrete query actually uses an available index.

MySQL 8.4 documents that each InnoDB table has a clustered index storing row data, that a defined primary key is used as the clustered index, and that each secondary-index record contains the row primary-key columns used to search the clustered index; long primary keys increase secondary-index space.

findings: The previous candidate overreached beyond its evidence mappings on FULLTEXT/SPATIAL details, constraint behavior, multi-column selection guidance, and covering-index behavior.
The current candidate separates DDL constraint/type labels, access-method syntax, and InnoDB storage organization instead of presenting them as one flat taxonomy.

MySQL 8.4 CREATE TABLE documentation supports the INDEX/KEY synonym, PRIMARY/UNIQUE/FULLTEXT/SPATIAL definitions, multiple key parts, USING BTREE/HASH grammar, and the storage-engine boundary for selectable index types.

MySQL 8.4 optimization documentation supports the row-location benefit and the space/write-maintenance cost of indexes; the answer avoids claiming that a specific SQL statement must use an index without an execution-plan check.
MySQL 8.4 InnoDB documentation supports clustered-index row storage, primary-key clustering, primary-key columns in secondary records, and the secondary-index space cost of long primary keys.

The revised text intentionally removes or bounds the prior unsupported claims about detailed FULLTEXT/SPATIAL behavior, universal composite-index ordering rules, constraint implementation details, and covering-index shortcuts.
